did_you_know.text: The Hebrew word for “holy” comes from a root that also means “set apart” or “dedicated.” In the Bible, holiness is therefore not only personal purity, but also a way of life devoted to God.
The Hebrew word translated as “fear” can also mean reverence or respect. The verse therefore calls for honoring parents, not merely obeying them.
Leaving grain behind created a kind of social safety net in the ancient world. The Book of Ruth describes Ruth gathering leftover grain to obtain food for herself and Naomi.
Alongside the poor, the Torah mentions the “ger,” a resident outsider living among the Israelites. This emphasizes that social support is not meant only for members of one’s own nation.
A day laborer in the ancient world might depend on that day’s pay to buy food. That is why the Torah warns employers not to delay payment, even until morning.
“Love your neighbor as yourself” became one of the most famous statements in Jewish ethics. In the Talmudic tradition, Hillel the Elder treated it as a central principle of the Torah.
In Jewish law, “shaatnez” became the specific name for a garment made from both wool and linen. It is an example of a biblical word receiving a precise technical meaning in later tradition.
The word “orlah” literally refers to a covering or foreskin, and here it describes fruit that is not yet available for eating. Even today, the laws of orlah concern fruit from young trees.

The words for “divination” and “soothsaying” refer to interpreting signs or times in order to predict the future. The prohibition distinguishes trust in God from attempts to control events through magic or omens.

In the Bible, gray hair is seen as a sign of age and experience and is therefore worthy of honor. Rising before an elder is a physical gesture that expresses respect for the person’s status and wisdom.

The word “ger” does not describe a passing visitor, but an outsider who has settled and lives within the community. The reason for treating such a person well is Israel’s own memory of being strangers in Egypt.

An ephah was a measure for dry goods, while a hin was a measure for liquids, though their exact sizes are uncertain. Mentioning them shows that ancient commerce used recognized systems of measurement.
